what: The CGPA to Percentage Converter turns a CGPA into a percentage, or a percentage into a CGPA, using the formula you choose. Each formula is written out next to the result so you can see exactly how the number was made.

It includes a simple proportional estimate for the 4.0 scale used in Pakistan, the CBSE × 9.5 rule, the formulas commonly quoted for VTU, Mumbai University and Anna University, and a custom formula for any other university. A clear note explains where each formula comes from and its limits.

There is no single universal formula. Your university's own rule or equivalence table is always the one that counts, so use this tool for a quick estimate and check the official figure before you submit a form.
uses: Fill in a job or admission form
Many forms ask for a percentage when your transcript shows a CGPA.
See if your CGPA meets a 60% or 75% cut-off for a scholarship, master's admission or job test.
Find the CGPA that matches a percentage, for example to compare with a CGPA requirement.
Switch formulas to see how much the answer changes between methods.
Enter its multiplier and offset in Custom.
tutorial: Click "CGPA → Percentage" or "Percentage → CGPA" at the top.
Open "Formula" and choose the one for your board or university. Read the note under the result: it explains the formula and when it applies.
Type your CGPA in "Your CGPA" or your percentage in "Your percentage (%)". The result appears straight away in the large box, with the formula used.
Use a custom formula if needed
Choose "Custom" and enter the "Multiplier", the "Offset" added after multiplying, and the "Highest possible CGPA". For example, a plain conversion on a 5.0 scale is multiplier 20 and offset 0.
Below the result, a table lists common CGPA values and their percentages for the chosen formula.
Click "Copy result" to copy the answer with the formula, ready to paste.
features: CGPA to percentage and percentage to CGPA with the same formula.
Simple 4.0 proportional, CBSE × 9.5, VTU (CGPA − 0.75) × 10, Mumbai University 7.1 × CGPA + 11, Anna University × 10.
Any multiplier, offset and maximum CGPA.
Each formula comes with a note on where it comes from and a reminder that official tables take priority.
A CGPA above the scale or a percentage the formula cannot produce is flagged instead of giving a wrong answer.
Common values for the chosen formula at a glance.

example.title: Worked example: the same grades, different formulas
example.text: A student in Pakistan has a CGPA of 3.2 out of 4. The simple proportional estimate gives 3.2 ÷ 4 × 100 = 80%, but their university's own equivalence table may give a different figure, so they check the transcript before using it. A student in India with an 8.0 CGPA on a 10-point scale gets 8 × 9.5 = 76% with the CBSE rule, (8 − 0.75) × 10 = 72.5% with the VTU formula, 7.1 × 8 + 11 = 67.8% with the Mumbai University formula, and 80% with the Anna University formula.

tips: Use the formula your own board or university gives. If your marksheet prints a conversion rule, use it in Custom.
In Pakistan, ask your university's examinations office for its official equivalence table or certificate when a form needs an exact percentage.
The CBSE × 9.5 rule was given for CBSE's CGPA grades; other universities may not accept it.
When applying abroad, many universities prefer your CGPA and grading scale as printed rather than a converted percentage.
Keep two decimals of your CGPA for a more accurate conversion.
problems: The result is different from my university's figure
Universities use their own formulas or tables. Choose Custom and enter your university's numbers, or use its official figure.
It says my CGPA is outside the range
Each formula is for one scale. A CGPA of 8 does not fit a 4.0 formula. Pick a formula for your scale, or Custom with the right maximum.
It says the percentage has no matching CGPA
Some formulas cannot reach every percentage. For example, Mumbai University's 7.1 × CGPA + 11 gives at most 82%, and CBSE × 9.5 at most 95%.
(CGPA − 0.75) × 10 is below zero for a CGPA under 0.75, so the formula does not apply there.
